questions.q: What does the lesson say the first 30 days of a new Salesforce role should mostly focus on?
options: Immediately rebuilding the security model
Deploying as much new automation as possible
Avoiding contact with other departments
Understanding what already exists -- stakeholders, the data model, and the security model -- before changing it
questions.explain: The lesson frames the first month as learning the organization -- people, data model, and security -- before making changes.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the actual goal of the small tasks taken on during days 30-60?
options: Building trust by listening to real pain points and fixing something real without breaking anything else
Proving you can rebuild the entire org alone
Avoiding any contact with existing tickets
Immediately proposing a full re-architecture
questions.explain: The lesson states the goal in this window is building trust through small, real fixes, not proving broad rebuilding ability.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say trying to re-architect everything in week one is a mistake?
options: Because re-architecture is never appropriate at any point in a role
Because new hires are not allowed to propose changes under any circumstances
Because even a genuinely flawed existing design usually has a reason, and you won't know that reason until you've been there long enough to ask the right people
Because it's against Salesforce's terms of service
questions.explain: The lesson explains that existing designs usually have context behind them that a new hire hasn't yet learned, which is why rushing to re-architect is risky.

questions.q: What does the lesson recommend over changing production directly to save time on something that feels small?
options: Skipping sandbox testing is fine as long as the change is small
Testing in a sandbox first, since "small" changes are often the ones that aren't as safe as they feel
Asking a coworker to make the change instead
Waiting exactly 90 days before making any change at all
questions.explain: The lesson lists changing production directly because something felt small as a common early mistake, implying sandbox testing should not be skipped.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a visible 'quick win' matters more than a long list of planned fixes?
options: Because planned fixes are against company policy
Because lists are technically impossible to create in Salesforce
Because a real, visible improvement builds credibility and gives you something concrete to reference later, unlike a list of intentions
Because quick wins are the only thing ever evaluated in a performance review
questions.explain: The lesson explains that a real, delivered improvement builds more trust and provides a concrete reference point than a list of things still only planned.
